title: Steffen Castle
text:
Researcher, DFKI Berlin · PhD Student, TU Berlin


I study how language models use information internally, and how those internal signals can be turned into tools for detecting hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, monitoring drift, and controlling generation.

text:
Research story


2019–2020
Improving neural network explanations
Master’s research at DFKI on Pattern-Guided Attribution and Pattern-Guided Integrated Gradients.


2020–2022
PLASS: information extraction for supply-chain risk
Relation extraction and uncertainty quantification for monitoring supply-chain risks in multilingual news (BMWi, with Siemens). Produced Detecting Covariate Drift with Explanations (2021): explanation signals as operational tools for detecting covariate shift.


2023
PhD: machine-internal uses of explainability
Thesis topic Beyond Human Interaction: Alternative Applications for Explanations. Rather than producing explanations for people to read, the thesis asks whether attribution signals can serve AI systems directly: detecting distribution shift, improving retrieval, and verifying factuality.


2023–2024
Data4Transparency: search over leaked documents for investigative journalists
Few-shot joint named-entity recognition and relation extraction to surface entities and relationships in large document dumps, with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP).


2024
Green-AI Hub: automated product carbon footprint estimation
LLM-based entity linking to map manufactured components to environmental impact databases for SMEs (Green-AI Hub Mittelstand, BMUV). Published at the Ecology & Environment NLP workshop, 2025.


2024–2025
Explaining embedding similarity for retrieval
Adapting attribution methods (ALTI, Integrated Gradients) to pairwise embedding similarity, and using token-level attributions to rerank retrieved documents for RAG.


2025–present
GenKI4Media: trustworthy generative AI for the media sector
Methods for the transparency, traceability, and accuracy of AI-generated editorial content (BMFTR, with dpa and Deutsche Welle). Two strands: detecting unsupported RAG answers from model internals (extended abstract at BlackboxNLP 2026, full paper forthcoming), and DELTA, training-free character-length control for masked diffusion LMs (EMNLP 2026).


2026
XPO (Software Campus): explainability-guided prompt repair
Project lead for a 12-month Software Campus project with Celonis on explainability-guided prompt optimization and repair for reliable agentic workflows.


2026
GUARDRAIL: reliability-aware knowledge graphs
Franco-German AI for Science project on propagating source-reliability signals from KG construction through retrieval, claim verification, and abstention.

title: Projects
text:
Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models, EMNLP 2026 (main conference)
This work grew out of GenKI4Media, where editorial partners such as dpa and Deutsche Welle need generated text to fit predefined display slots. Summarization with a fixed character length matters for headlines, article previews, notifications, subtitles, and UI text, where even a few extra characters cause truncation or layout overflow. Autoregressive models struggle with precise character-length control: training-based methods need task-specific fine-tuning, and zero-shot prompting only achieves approximate compliance.
DELTA (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm) is a training-free, inference-time method for masked diffusion LMs. At each denoising step it estimates the expected character length of the output and dynamically inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward the target length. It requires no fine-tuning and works with off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs (e.g. LLaDA, Dream).
Across three summarization benchmarks, DELTA reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality in both automatic and human evaluation.
PDF

title: Projects
text:
Hallucination detection from model internals
Ongoing work within GenKI4Media on detecting contextual hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation from the model’s internal computation. When a language model answers from a retrieved document, its attention heads mix evidence from the context with evidence from the model’s own self-generated tokens. Separating these contributions inside the residual stream yields signals of whether a generated answer is actually supported by the source, both as a training-free groundedness readout and as a supervised hallucination detector.
An extended abstract of this work appears at BlackboxNLP 2026 (co-located with EMNLP 2026); a full paper is forthcoming.

Why it matters
For scientific and high-stakes RAG systems, the practical question is often not only whether an answer sounds true, but whether each claim is grounded in the documents provided to the model.


Poster
This project was adapted into a collaboration-oriented poster for the AI Grid Summer School “AI for Science”, Paris 2026.

title: Projects
text:
GUARDRAIL
Grounded Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning with Deferrable, Reliable Abstention In LLMs
A Franco-German project proposal developed at the AI For Science 2026 Summer School (AI Grid · DataIA · SCAI), which I coordinate. Partners: DFKI Berlin, University of Bamberg (Cognitive Systems), Lamarr Institute / University of Bonn, Université Paris-Saclay, and INRAE MaIAGE.
Knowledge graphs enable symbolic fact-checking of LLMs, but current approaches assume the graph itself is reliable. When LLMs are used to build the graph, converting probabilistic outputs into discrete triples strips away the signal of how well each fact is supported by its source, so a KG can end up validating hallucinated claims instead of preventing them.
GUARDRAIL studies the end-to-end propagation of reliability signals in KG-grounded LLM reasoning for environmental data:

Uncertainty-aware KG construction: retain source-groundedness (from interpretability-based source attribution) and citation-network quality signals alongside each extracted triple.
Reliability-aware retrieval and claim verification: adapt graph-based retrieval and KG-grounded verification to use these signals, evaluated on climate-related claim verification (ClimateCheck).
Calibrated abstention: combine graph reliability, retrieval coverage, and model confidence into an answer-or-defer policy, with a secondary transfer to plant- and pest-related QA.

title: Projects
text:
GenKI4Media
Generative AI assistants for the media, cultural and creative sectors (BMFTR, 2025–present)
A consortium project with 3pc, ART+COM, Fraunhofer FOKUS, dpa, and Deutsche Welle building generative AI assistants for editorial work. DFKI’s sub-project develops methods to improve the transparency, traceability, and trustworthiness of AI-generated content: relating generated text to external sources, validating it against them, and correcting it where necessary. My work in the project covers hallucination detection from model internals and length-controlled summarization with diffusion LMs (see above).

title: Projects
text:
Data4Transparency
Information extraction for investigative journalism (2023–2024, with OCCRP)
Investigative journalists working with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project receive large leaked document collections with little labelled data. This project developed enhanced search over such document dumps using few-shot joint named-entity recognition and relation extraction, so that entities and their connections can be surfaced at scale.

title: Projects

PLASS: explanation-based drift detection
Platform for Analytical Supply Chain Management Services (BMWi, 2020–2022, led by Siemens)
PLASS built a B2B platform for AI-based supply-chain risk monitoring, extracting decision-relevant information from multilingual news. My work covered relation extraction and, in particular, how explanation signals can identify covariate drift in deployed models, using interpretability methods as practical model-monitoring tools rather than only as human-facing explanations (Detecting Covariate Drift with Explanations, NLPCC XAI workshop 2021). title: Research
text:
Research agenda
I am interested in explanations as operational signals: not only as post-hoc descriptions for humans, but as measurable quantities that can improve AI systems.
Current directions:

detecting contextual hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation,
using model-internal features for evaluation and reliability,
controllable generation with masked diffusion language models,
explanation-based covariate drift detection,
interpretable NLP systems for information extraction and document understanding,
reliable AI workflows for science and industry.

title: Research
text:
PhD thesis
Beyond Human Interaction: Alternative Applications for Explanations (TU Berlin / DFKI, since 2023)
Traditional XAI produces explanations for humans to read. My thesis instead treats attribution methods (Integrated Gradients, ALTI, LRP, and mechanistic decompositions of the residual stream) as internal signals that an AI system can consume itself. It is organised around three questions:

Can explanations detect when the input distribution changes? Attribution patterns shift before performance drops, enabling label-free drift detection.
Can explanations improve retrieval in RAG systems? Token-level attribution for pairwise embedding similarity, and attribution-based reranking of retrieved documents.
Can explanations verify factuality? Tracking which source tokens influence each generated token to detect contextual hallucinations and attach citations.

title: Research
text:
Explainability as an engineering signal
A recurring theme in my work is that explanations can be used to improve AI systems, not only to explain them after the fact. This includes model monitoring, drift detection, model evaluation, and mechanistic diagnostics.

title: Research
text:
Collaboration interests
I am especially interested in source-grounded AI-for-science settings where model outputs should be constrained by provided evidence:

mathematical or scientific reasoning,
engineering and technical documentation,
policy, legal, and financial reports,
enterprise process and operational documents.
